title: Who Is Asha Sharma? The Wisconsin-Born Executive Who Never Made a Video Game — and Is Now Running Xbox
excerpt: Seven months after Microsoft handed her the Xbox controller, the former Instacart COO is cutting thousands of jobs, cutting Game Pass prices, and telling hard truths — guided by a mantra from her immigrant upbringing: clarity is kindness.
body:
The surprise pick

When Microsoft announced on February 20, 2026, that Phil Spencer was retiring after nearly four decades and handing the Xbox business to Asha Sharma, the gaming world did a double take. Sharma, then president of Microsoft's CoreAI product division, had never worked in video games. She leapfrogged Spencer's heir apparent, Sarah Bond, who departed the company in the same shake-up. Forums and podcasts filled with the same question: who is Asha Sharma?

Seven months later, the answer is coming into focus — and it is a blunt one. Sharma has cut thousands of jobs, spun off game studios, slashed the price of Game Pass, and told employees the business is "not healthy." This week, The Wall Street Journal profiled her as "The Woman Fixing a Microsoft Mess With Brutal Honesty."

Racine roots

Sharma was born in 1989 in Racine, Wisconsin, the second of five siblings, to parents of Indian descent who had immigrated to the United States from New Zealand and settled near relatives. Her parents later divorced. Her mother worked at a department store; her father put himself through an engineering degree while working at a family-owned metal fabrication business. Sharma has credited her father's work ethic with shaping her own attitude toward school, work, and everything after.

As a teenager, she worked on a golf course, earned a second-degree black belt in taekwondo, and studied business at the University of Minnesota's Carlson School of Management, graduating in 2011 — completing research projects in Hungary and Poland, helping establish a nonprofit that raised around $500,000, and launching a center for at-risk teenagers in Brooklyn Park, Minnesota.

From marketing to Messenger to a $42 IPO

Sharma started working at age 17 at consumer-goods maker S.C. Johnson. After graduation she joined Microsoft in marketing (2011–2013), then jumped to the home-services startup Porch, where she rose to chief operating officer and landed on Forbes' 30 Under 30 list.

In 2017 she joined Facebook — now Meta — as vice president of product and engineering, running Messenger, Instagram Direct, and the company's calling and video products at planetary scale. In February 2021 she became chief operating officer of Instacart, steering the grocery-delivery company through its September 2023 IPO at $42 a share and a turn to profitability.

She returned to Microsoft in February 2024 as president of the CoreAI division, overseeing AI models, developer tools, and responsible-AI work — which made her, in CEO Satya Nadella's telling, the right person to fix a gaming business whose console sales were sliding.

Why she matters now

The Journal profile, published September 12, paints the stakes: Xbox generates roughly $23 billion in revenue, but the number is declining; some 14,000 employees operate on margins of just three percent; Game Pass has missed its growth projections. Sharma's operating mantra, which she repeats to colleagues, is "clarity is kindness."

"Great companies are incredibly comfortable sharing successes and sharing wins. Every company needs to be better at sharing hard things and clear realities." — Asha Sharma, at a Minecraft studio town hall

She runs the division from what the Journal describes as a modest office by C-suite standards, and she reportedly spends hours personally working through player support tickets. Her first message to Xbox staff set the tone: the company would "not chase short-term efficiency or flood our ecosystem with soulless AI slop," declaring that "games are and always will be art, crafted by humans."

The actions have matched the rhetoric. She lowered the price of Xbox Game Pass Ultimate — a move IGN praised as a key first step toward redemption — wound down Copilot on Xbox consoles, ended the "This is an Xbox" marketing campaign, and restored the Xbox name after a brief "Microsoft Gaming" rebrand. In July, she announced what she called the most significant restructure in Xbox history: about 3,200 job cuts across fiscal 2027, including 1,600 immediate eliminations, with Compulsion Games and Double Fine becoming independent, Ninja Theory and Undead Labs moving to new ownership, and Arkane in consultation over a sale or spin-off. In June, she was appointed to the Federal Reserve's Productivity and Jobs Task Force advising on AI's economic impact.

A diaspora milestone — with friction

Sharma joins a lengthening roll call of Indian-origin executives running the world's biggest companies — Nadella at Microsoft, Sundar Pichai at Alphabet, Nikesh Arora at Palo Alto Networks, and now Anil Chakravarthy succeeding Shantanu Narayen at Adobe. She cites Indian-American businesswoman Indra Nooyi as an inspiration, and she is open about the juggle: married with a blended family of three children, she has spoken about how raising a family taught her to become more comfortable with uncertainty.

But her appointment also exposed an uglier current. Despite being born and raised in Wisconsin, Sharma became a target of racist online backlash, with some voices recycling claims of corporate nepotism and casting her as part of an "Indian tech-bro" archetype — a referendum on Indian-American identity that The Videshi covered in July. It is a telling coda: even at the very top of American corporate life, the diaspora's success still has to be defended.

And in a final detail that captures her approach: having never been a gamer, Sharma created an Xbox gamertag — AMRAHSAHSA — and started playing, telling followers she did it simply to "learn and understand this world." For a CEO famous for brutal honesty, it may be the most honest onboarding plan in corporate America.
image_caption: Asha Sharma at the 2026 Xbox Showcase. She became CEO of Microsoft Gaming in February 2026, succeeding Phil Spencer.
nri_angle: Sharma's rise to the top of Xbox — and the racist backlash her appointment drew despite her Wisconsin birth — captures both the ascent and the friction of Indian-American leadership in 2026.
author: Diaspora Desk
